surveys.narrative:
Burntside Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large and deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (unmineralized) water. Burntside Lake is smaller and has clearer water than most of the lakes in this lake class.

Burntside Lake was thermally stratified on 07/16/2007 with surface temperatures of 69 F and bottom temperatures of 43 F. Good oxygen for trout (more than 5 ppm) was retained to the bottom in each of the three major basins (North Arm, East End, West End) of this lake. The water quality in 2007 was similar to previous investigations on this lake that showed Burntside Lake was oligotrophic with excellent water quality and low water fertility.

Fish populations in 2007 were investigated with stratified shallow and deep gillnets, and with deep smelt gillnets. Twelve of each type of gillnet were set, but one of each type was disturbed by the public, leaving eleven of each net type with usable data. Trapnets were not used to sample shallow water fish populations in 2007 due to staffing constraints and because previous trapnetting in this lake captured low numbers of fish of the same species and in the same proportions as the gillnet catch.

SHALLOW WATER FISH POPULATIONS

The shallow gillnets were set in and above the thermocline at an average depth of 9 ft for the shallow end of the net and an average depth of 20 ft for the deep end of the net. On average, the water temperature at both the shallow and the deep ends of the nets was 68 F, although some nets tailed off into 30 ft deep water where the temperature was 57 F. Fifteen previous shallow water investigations were conducted on Burntside Lake dating back to 1950, with 10-19 shallow gillnets used in each investigation. Shallow water fish populations in 2007, as in previous investigations on this lake, were dominated by walleye, northern pike, smallmouth bass, and rock bass. Fish catch quartiles have not been developed for stratified gillnets, so no comparison can be made with other Lake Class 2 lakes.

Walleye have been stocked in Burntside Lake since 1911, and walleye fingerlings have been stocked every-other-year in Burntside Lake since 1988. Walleye numbers in 2007 (4.2/gillnet) were lower than in recent investigations on this lake, but were similar to the median catch of 4.4/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Walleye sizes in 2007 averaged 18.0" (2.9 lb), which was larger than the average size of 15.7" in all investigations on this lake. All but two of the walleye captured in 2007 appeared to be from fingerling-stocked year classes. The two walleye that appeared to be from a non-stocked year class, both age six, were the same size as the age seven fish, indicating their assigned ages may have been in error and that they may have been from a stocked year. Scales of older walleye in Burntside Lake are difficult to read, and inconsistencies such as this sometimes occur. Except for the age one walleye that were stocked as fingerlings the previous fall, the older walleye were very plump, with lots of visceral fat, and growth was very fast (in the fourth quartile, by area standards). Thirty of 42 walleye stomachs examined were empty, eight contained smelt, three contained unidentified fish remains, and one contained a sculpin.

Northern pike numbers in 2007 (2.7/gillnet) were higher than the median catch of 1.7/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Pike sizes in 2007 averaged 23.9" (3.5 lb), which was similar to the average size of 23.6" in all investigations on this lake. The largest pike captured in 2007 (caught in a deep gillnet) was 33.5". Pike scales were difficult to read, resulting in conflicting data on age and growth. Twenty two of 28 pike stomachs examined were empty, the remainder contained fish including yellow perch, smallmouth bass, rock bass, and smelt.

Smallmouth bass numbers in 2007 (1.7/gillnet) were higher than the median catch of 1.4/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Smallmouth sizes in 2007 averaged 12.2" (1.2 lb), which was similar to the average size of 11.7" in all investigations on this lake. The largest smallmouth was 18.7". Four of six smallmouth stomachs examined were empty, and two contained crayfish.

Some of the northern pike, smallmouth bass, and walleye captured in 2007 were infected with neascus and yellow grub. Some of the smallmouth bass were also infected with bass tapeworm larvae in their viscera. Neascus (black spot), yellow grub, and bass tapeworm are all common parasites that are native to the area. They cannot infect humans, are often removed by filleting fish, and are killed at temperatures used to cook fish.

SMELT POPULATION

Rainbow smelt were first observed in Burntside Lake in 1970 and a variety of nets were used to catch smelt through the mid 1980's. Regular smelt assessment gillnetting began in 1987 at standard locations (two nets in each of the three basins on Burntside Lake: North Arm, East End, West End), with nets that were 6 ft x 100 ft x 1/2" bar mesh multifilament nylon, and 6 ft x 150 ft or 200 ft x 3/8" bar mesh multifilament nylon. Standard smelt nets (200 ft x 6 ft, with one 100 ft panel of 3/8" bar mesh multifilament nylon and one 100 ft panel of 1/2" bar mesh multifilament nylon) were introduced in 1992 and previous 3/8" bar mesh net catches were converted to 100 ft equivalents for purposes of comparison with the new nets. Two mid-depth smelt nets were added to each basin in 1998 to ensure that the entire water column from the thermocline (at about 30 ft) to very deep water was sampled.

These smelt gillnet investigations showed that smelt catches averaged 130/standard smelt net from 1987 through 1995. Smelt numbers declined from 1996 through 2005, averaging 35/standard smelt net, but then rebounded to 128/smelt net in 2006 and 140/standard smelt net in 2007.

In most investigations on Burntside Lake, smelt numbers were highest in the East End and lowest in the North Arm. In 2006 and 2007, however, smelt numbers were evenly distributed in each of the three basins of Burntside Lake. As in most recent investigations on this lake, most of the smelt captured in 2007 (99 percent) were caught in the 3/8" bar mesh. Smelt sizes in 2005 averaged 4.9"; the largest was 8.2".

Also captured in the smelt gillnets in 2007 were 11 slimy sculpin and three lake trout. One of the lake trout (5.9") had no fin clips, indicating it was produced naturally. The two larger trout (12.2", right ventral clip; 19.5", left ventral clip) had been stocked as yearlings in 2004 and 2000, respectively.

OTHER COLD WATER FISH POPULATIONS

Lake trout have been stocked into Burntside Lake since 1916. Since 1988 about 70,000 Gillis Lake strain lake trout yearlings have been stocked in Burntside Lake every other year. Since 1984 all stocked lake trout have been fin-clipped for later identification, to determine their survival and growth, and to monitor for the presence of unclipped trout that were produced by natural reproduction.

Lake trout numbers in 2007 (2.2/gillnet) were identical to the median catch of 2.2/gillnet in all deep water investigations on this lake. By weight, the lake trout catch in 2007 of 2.3 lb/gillnet was lower than the median catch of 3.2 lb/gillnet in all deep water investigations on this lake. Lake trout sizes in 2007 averaged 13.2" (1.0 lb), which was smaller than the average size of 14.5" in all investigations on this lake. The largest lake trout captured in 2007 was 23.2". Nine of 22 lake trout stomachs examined in 2007 were empty, eight contained smelt, four contained slimy sculpins, and one contained invertebrate remains. A few of the lake trout had anchor worms attached to them. Anchor worms are common parasites of fish and do not harm humans.

Of the 26 lake trout captured in the standard deep gillnets and the smelt nets in 2005, 12 were fin clipped, indicating they had been stocked. The 14 unclipped lake trout were aged by sectioning their otoliths, but the otoliths often broke before the sectioning was completed and the confidence of the reader was low for some fish.

Of the fourteen unclipped lake trout, one trout (5.9") was age 1+ from the 2006 year class, eight trout averaging 12.1" (range: 11.3-13.2") were age 3+ from the 2004 year class, three trout averaging 17.6" (range: 16.4-19.5") were age 4+ from the 2003 year class, and two trout were age 5 or older (19.5", 21.9"). Growth of the age 1-3 trout was typical for this lake, but growth of the age 4 and 5+ trout was substantially faster than typical, indicating that there may have been a problem with the ageing as mentioned in the previous paragraph.

The presence of young, unclipped trout indicates that natural recruitment of lake trout is occurring. The proportion of naturally produced lake trout in the deep gillnet and smelt gillnet catches has increased in recent investigations, from 11 percent (3 of 27) in 2001, to 23 percent (6 of 26) in 2003, 33 percent (9 of 27) in 2005, and 54 percent (14 of 26) in 2007.

Ten of the 12 fin-clipped lake trout had clips identifying year classes that could reasonably be assigned to the fish based on their lengths. Seven trout were age 2+ from the 2005 year class stocked in 2006 and averaged 9.1" (range: 7.9-11.0"). Three trout were age 4+ from the 2003 year class stocked in 2004 and averaged 13.9" (range: 12.2-15.3"). Two larger trout (19.5", 23.2") had clips that did not reasonably match with their size.

Considering both stocked and naturally produced lake trout in Burntside Lake, age 1+ and 2+ lake trout growth rates were typical for lake trout lakes in the Tower Fisheries Management Area, while age 3+ and older growth rates were faster than normal. The faster growth of older trout may be due to the abundant smelt population available as forage.

The lake whitefish population in 2007 continued a trend of nonexistent recruitment, resulting in declining numbers and increasing sizes. Whitefish numbers in Burntside Lake averaged 9.5/deep gillnet from 1950 through 1981, declined to an average of 5.2/deep gillnet through 1985, then gradually declined to the 2007 catch of 1.3/gillnet. Whitefish sizes gradually increased during this time, from an average of 14.1" in the first two investigations, to an average of 24.5" in 2007. No whitefish under 22" were caught in 2007.

Cisco have apparently been extirpated from Burntside Lake. An average of 4.1 cisco/deep gillnet were captured from 1950 through 1986. Cisco numbers then gradually declined, and no cisco have been captured in the last five deep water gillnet assessments.

We feel that the unintentional introduction of smelt has resulted in the nearly total failure of natural recruitment of walleye, lake whitefish, and cisco in Burntside Lake. Lake trout natural reproduction was also poor and has only recently showed some signs of rebounding. These are all cold water spawning species that do not nest or otherwise protect their eggs or young following spawning. The literature has many examples of similar recruitment failures for cold water spawning fish in lakes stocked with smelt (e.g. Evans and Loftus, 1987. Colonization of Inland Lakes in the Great Lakes Region by Rainbow Smelt. International Symposium of Stocks Assessment and Yield Prediction. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences. Vol. 44, Supplement 2:249-266). The mechanisms by which smelt affect recruitment of other species may be direct (by preying on eggs or young fish) or indirect (by competing with these species for forage, particularly invertebrate forage).

Burntside Lake was thermally stratified on 07/18/2006 with surface temperatures of 75 F and bottom temperatures of 44 F. Adequate oxygen for trout (more than 5 ppm) was retained to within five feet of the bottom in each of the three major basins (North Arm, East End, West End) of this lake. The water quality in 2006 was similar to previous investigations on this lake that showed Burntside Lake was an oligotrophic lake with excellent water quality and low water fertility.

Smelt were first observed in Burntside Lake in 1970 and a variety of nets were used to catch smelt through the mid 1980's. Regular smelt assessment gillnetting began in 1987 at standard locations (two nets in each of the three major basins on the lake) with nets that were 6 feet x 100 feet x 0.5 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon and 6 feet x 150 feet or 200 feet x 0.375 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon. Standard smelt nets (200 feet x 6 feet with one 100 foot panel of 0.375 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon and one 100 foot panel of 0.5 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon) were introduced in 1992 and previous 0.375 inch bar mesh catches were converted to 100 foot equivalents for purposes of comparison with the new nets. Two mid depth smelt nets were added to each major basin in 1998 to ensure that the entire water column from the thermocline (at about 25 feet) to deep water was sampled.

These smelt investigations showed that smelt catches averaged 130/standard smelt net through the mid 1990's. Smelt numbers then declined, averaging 35/standard smelt net from 1996 through 2005 (the 2005 smelt catch was 12/standard smelt net). This decline appeared to show that our strategy of stocking walleye fingerlings and lake trout yearlings was reducing the smelt population through predation. In 2006, however, the smelt catch of 127/standard smelt net rebounded to levels not seen in a decade. The distribution of smelt within the major basins of the lake was similar to recent investigations. The highest catch of smelt (164/standard smelt net) was in the West End, followed by 141/standard smelt net in the East End, and 78/standard smelt net in the North Arm.

Similar to most recent assessments, 99 percent (1,509 of 1,530) of the smelt captured in 2006 were in the 0.375 inch bar mesh. Smelt sizes in 2006 averaged 4.8 inches. The largest smelt was 8.4 inches.

Also captured in the smelt nets in 2006 were six lake trout and six slimy sculpin. All of the lake trout had clipped fins, indicating they had been stocked. Four of the lake trout, averaging 6.1 inches, had adipose and right ventral fin clips and had been stocked two months earlier as yearlings. One trout (23.0 inches) had adipose and left ventral fin clips and had likely been stocked as a yearling in the spring of 2000. One trout (15.7 inches) had adipose and right pectoral fin clips. Trout stocked in Burntside Lake have not had pectoral fins clipped since 1990. This trout could have been stocked as a yearling in 2002 (marked with an adipose fin clip) and had a deformed or damaged right pectoral fin that made the right pectoral fin appear it had been clipped.

Burntside Lake is a 7313-acre lake with a maximum depth of 126 feet located four miles northeast of Ely in northeastern St. Louis County. Based on physical and chemical characteristics, Minnesota's lakes are categorized into 43 lake classes. Burntside Lake is in lake class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large and deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (low mineral content) water. Burntside Lake is smaller and has clearer water than most of the lakes in this lake class. Several lakes in this lake class, including Knife, Basswood, and Trout have lake trout as a member of the fish community.

Fish populations in 2011 were investigated using a combination of 12 standard deep gill net sets, 11 shallow gill nets, and 11 standard small mesh gill net sets. The purpose of the investigation was to sample all species in Burntside Lake.

Cold Water Fish Populations

Lake trout have been stocked in Burntside Lake since 1916. Since 1988, about 70,000 Gillis Lake strain lake trout yearlings have been stocked in Burntside Lake every other year. Since 1984, all stocked lake trout have been fin-clipped for later identification, to determine their survival and growth, and to distinguish them from trout that were produced by natural reproduction.

In 2011, lake trout abundance based on deep gill nets was below the historic average. Twenty-five percent of the 16 lake trout sampled were not clipped. The proportion of naturally produced trout had increased from 11% (3 of 27) in 2001, to 23% (6 of 26) in 2003, 33% (9 of 27) in 2005, and 54% (14 of 26) in 2007 and then decreased in 2009 to 14% (3 of 21) In 2010, lake trout stocking was discontinued. Currently, Burntside Lake is on a frequent assessment schedule so changes to the fishery can be monitored.

In 2011 captured lake trout varied in length from 8.7 to 32.6 inches with a mean length and weight of 13.8 inches and 1.7 pounds. The 32.6-inch lake trout was the largest captured of any assessment. The mean length was slightly below the 2009 findings (15.0 inches) and the historic average (14.5 inches). Besides the 2007 and 2009 stocking year classes, other year classes identified were 2007 (age seven) and 2005 (age six) year classes. Most lake trout sampled were stocked clipped fish with 50% from the 2009 stocking. Overall, when lake trout became older and bigger, they started to target smelt as forage and subsequently grew at a faster rate.

A special assessment targeting spawning lake trout was conducted in October 2011. Lake trout sampled in this assessment were used in a genetic study to help better understand which strain of lake trout is successfully spawning. Of the 57 mature lake trout captured, eight were fin-clipped.

Lake whitefish abundance has been decreasing since the earliest assessments and was at its lowest abundance in 2011. Along with this decrease in abundance, there has been an increase in size. The average mean length of the first two investigations was 14.1 inches and increased to an average of 24.4 inches in 2011. The smaller average lengths in earlier investigations reflect a younger population. Ages of whitefish in 2011 ranged from 31 to 45 years confirming an older population with no young fish entering the population. It is suspected that smelt are preying on young whitefish.

Cisco (tullibee) apparently has become extinct in Burntside Lake. In earlier assessments, cisco were quite common in the nets, however since 1997, no cisco has been captured. It is felt that the unintentional introduction of smelt has resulted in the nearly total failure of natural reproduction of walleye, whitefish, and cisco in Burntside Lake. Lake trout natural reproduction was also poor and has only recently showed signs of rebounding. All of these species do not nest or otherwise protect their eggs or young following spawning. Studies showed that smelt may directly affect natural reproduction of other species by preying on eggs or young fish or indirectly by competing with these fish for forage food.

Rainbow smelt were first observed in Burntside Lake in 1970, and a variety of nets were employed to catch smelt through the mid 1980's. Regular standard small mesh smelt assessment gillnetting began in 1987 at standard locations in all three arms of the lake. Smelt catches averaged 130/net from 1987 through 1995. Smelt numbers declined from 1996 through 2005, averaging 35/net, but then rebounded to 128 in 2006 and 140 in 2007. Smelt numbers were lower in 2008 and 2009 at 63.3 and 78.4 /smelt net. In 2011, smelt abundance of 7.0/net was the lowest since 1998 at 5.7/ net.

In most investigations on Burntside Lake, smelt numbers were highest in the East Arm and lowest in the North Arm. However, in 2006, 2007, and 2008, smelt numbers were evenly distributed in each of the three basins of Burntside Lake. Smelt numbers in both 2009 and 2011 were highest in the East Arm and lowest in the North Arm.

Cool water Fish Populations

In 2011, walleye abundance was above the 2007 findings. Abundance was also above the historic average. Since walleye stocking was initiated in 1979, abundance has improved. Walleye mean length of 16.4 inches was comparable to the historic average of 15.8 inches. Burntside walleye were growing well. At age three, Burntside walleye were 13.5 inches long compared to the Tower area lake class 2 mean of 11.3 inches. In 2011, only four of the 69 walleye sampled were from non-stocked years. The strongest year class was from 2008, a stocked year, composing 45% of the catch.

Northern pike abundance was comparable to the historic average but down from 2007 findings. In 2011, northern pike length and weight was 24.0 inches and 3.5 pounds. Pike over 40 inches were captured in past assessments.

Smallmouth bass abundance was the highest of any assessment. In 2011, smallmouth bass mean length was 13.7 inches. The largest smallmouth bass captured was 20.0 inches and was only topped by one captured in 1999 of 20.3 inches.

Burntside Lake is located northwest of Ely and has five public motorboat accesses as well as a number of portage and water route connections to other nearby lakes. It is a 7,314-acre lake with a maximum depth of 126 feet and clear water. There are several relatively minor inlets, located mostly on the north side of the lake, and the outlet is the Shagawa River, which flows out of the southwest corner of the lake where it then turns and heads east to Shagawa Lake. Burntside Lake is a two-story fishery with deep, cold, well oxygenated water capable of supporting a cold water fishery (fish such as lake trout, lake whitefish, cisco, and burbot) and a shallow, warmer, but still well oxygenated area capable of supporting a cool and warm water fishery (fish such as walleye, northern pike, bass and panfish).

Unfortunately, the fish community is affected by two non-native invasive species, rainbow smelt and spiny water flea. Rainbow smelt were first discovered in the lake in 1970. Their presence is likely a result of an unintended bait release or the consequence of smelt netters cleaning their catch from Lake Superior on their docks and unintentionally introducing fertilized eggs to the lake. Spiny water flea is a zooplankton species that was first discovered in Burntside Lake in 2010. Their presence is likely a result of infested boats or fishing equipment being used on Burntside. Spiny water flea are spread easily becuase they can attach to fishing lines, downriggers, anchor ropes, and fishing nets, as well as be transported in bait buckets, bilges, and livewells of boats if they are not completely dried out.

Burntside is one of the most popular lakes in the Tower area providing a number of recreational pursuits. It is a prototypical northern Minnesota/Canadian shield waterbody with shorelines covered in tall pines, areas of tall granite ledge rock, many islands, exceptionally clear water, and much of the shoreline is undeveloped. Areas along the south shore, east end, and parts of the north arm are accessible by road. Some of these areas are moderately developed with homes and cabins. Most of the undeveloped public land is owned by the US Forest Service. Several lakeshore campsites are located on the north arm and west end. In the spring of 2015 the Forest Service conducted prescribed burns along the north shore of much of the west end and part of the southwest side of the north arm. Some of the islands on the west end were also burned. Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline are mostly boulder and ledgerock. Some bays have soft bottoms with a fair amount of aquatic vegetation. Additionally, a few bays are quite sandy and make for great swimming areas.

Burntside has a long history of stocking dating back to 1912. Since 1965, walleye and lake trout were the only species that were stocked. Lake trout were stocked from the 1990's to 2010. Walleye fingerlings are still currently being stocked in even years at around 25,000 fish per stocking.

This survey used four different net types: deep water gillnets, shallow water gillnets, small mesh gillnets, and trap nets. Fish species sampled included black crappie, bluegill, burbot, golden shiner, deepwater sculpin, green sunfish, hybrid sunfish, lake trout, lake whitefish, northern pike, rainbow smelt, rock bass, slimy sculpin, shorthead redhorse, smallmouth bass, walleye, white sucker, and yellow perch.

The deep water gillnet catch for lake trout was almost two fish per net. This catch rate was similar to recent surveys on Burntside Lake and just below average when compared to other area lake trout lakes. Fish from 11 to 27 inches were sampled with an average length of nearly 18 inches. The largest fish sampled and the average length are on par with previous surveys. Lake trout stocking on Burntside Lake ended in 2010, and the ages of sampled fish indicate a healthy population with natural reproduction occurring on a regular basis.

Lake whitefish in Burntside first started showing declines starting in 1982 and the 2015 catch rate was the lowest on record. Since then, catch rates have increased gradually, and deep water gillnets sampled over 1 fish per net in 2024. Sizes ranged from 15 to 23 inches with an average of 18 inches. Ages ranged from 5 to 40 years old, indicating that natural reproduction has improved in recent years.

Unlike whitefish, the outlook for cisco (tullibee) has not improved in recent years. Cisco catch rates declined gradually from 1986 to 1997, when the last cisco was sampled in the lake. The declines in both cisco and whitefish catches coincide with the introduction of rainbow smelt in the lake. While recent surveys provide reason for optimism towards whitefish, it is assumed that cisco are no longer present in Burntside Lake.

Four burbot were sampled in deep water gillnets, which is average for Burntside Lake. Lengths were 18 to 26 inches with an average length of 22 inches. Although cisco seem to have disappeared and lake whitefish catch rates have varied, the burbot catch has remained relatively stable through time.

The walleye catch rate in 2024 was almost three fish per net, which was slightly lower than the historic average for the lake. Lengths ranged from 11 to 24 inches with an average of 17 inches which was slightly better than the average. Walleye growth in Burntside Lake is exceptional, likely due to the presence of smelt as a forage. Fish from 2 to 17 years old were sampled, and walleye averaged just over 16 inches by age 4.

The northern pike shallow water gillnet catch was three fish per net which is better than average for Burntside Lake. Lengths ranged from 12 to 32 inches with an average of 22 inches. Both the average and maximum lengths were on par with previous surveys.

Smallmouth bass were sampled in both shallow gillnets and trap nets. The gillnet catch rate was over one fish per net, which was average for the lake. Trap net catch rates were the lowest on record for the lake. Lengths ranged from 7 to over 20 inches with an average of 14 inches. Ages ranged from 1 to 12 years.

The bluegill trap net catch in 2024 was about five fish per net which is slightly higher than average for the lake. Sizes ranged from 4 to almost 9 inches with an average of almost 6.5 inches. Bluegill growth was relatively fast compared to other lakes in the Tower area, with fish exceeding 5 inches by age 4.

The yellow perch shallow gillnet catch was 1.5 fish per net which is slightly above average for the lake. The lengths ranged from 5 to 10 inches. These sizes are comparable to previous surveys.

Rainbow smelt are a non-native invasive fish that were first documented in Burntside Lake in 1970. Regular small-mesh gillnetting began in 1987. Previous surveys of smelt catches were highly variable but more recent assessments are showing lower numbers. The 2015 assessment shows the lowest catch rate to date. Sizes have remained relatively constant through time though. It is likely that the unintentional introduction of smelt has resulted in reduced natural reproduction for walleye and the complete disappearance of cisco from Burntside Lake. Lake trout and lake whitefish natural reproduction were also poor and have only recently showed signs of rebounding. These are all species that do not nest or otherwise protect their eggs or young following spawning. Smelt have been shown to have effects on these other species both by preying on eggs or young fish and by competing with these species for food.

Spiny water flea (Bythotrephes longimanus) are a non-native invasive zooplankton that were first discovered in Burntside Lake in 2010. They are known to consume other native zooplankton which are often an important food source for native fish. Evidence from other lakes has shown a decline or elimination of some species of native zooplankton after spinys were introduced. We encourage anglers to help prevent the spread of this invasive by completely drying out fishing lines, downriggers, anchor ropes, fishing nets,bait buckets, bilges and livewells. Although they were only recently introduced to Burntside Lake, their impacts have yet to be determined.

Burntside Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large and deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (low mineral content) water. Burntside Lake is smaller and has clearer water than most of the lakes in this lake class.

Burntside Lake was thermally stratified on 07/20/2009 with a surface temperature of 64 �F and a bottom temperature of 45 �F. Good oxygen for trout (more than 5 ppm) was retained to the bottom in each of the three major basins (North Arm, East End, West End) of this lake. The water quality in 2009 was similar to previous investigations on this lake that showed Burntside Lake was oligotrophic with excellent water quality and low fertility.

Fish populations in 2009 were investigated with 12 standard deep gillnet sets and 12 deep small mesh gillnet sets. The purpose of the investigation was to assess deep water fish populations, including an evaluation of the growth and survival of stocked lake trout and the relative contribution of lake trout natural reproduction. Annual small mesh gillnet sets was part of an ongoing rainbow smelt monitoring effort.

SMELT POPULATION

Rainbow smelt were first observed in Burntside Lake in 1970 and a variety of nets were used to catch smelt through the mid 1980's. Regular smelt assessment gillnetting began in 1987 at standard locations (two nets in each of the three basins on Burntside Lake: North Arm, East End, West End), with nets that were 6 ft x 100 ft x 1/2" bar mesh multifilament nylon, and 6 ft x 150 ft or 200 ft x 3/8" bar mesh multifilament nylon. Standard smelt nets (200 ft x 6 ft, with one 100 ft panel of 3/8" bar mesh multifilament nylon and one 100 ft panel of 1/2" bar mesh multifilament nylon) were introduced in 1992 and previous 3/8" bar mesh net catches were converted to 100 ft equivalents for purposes of comparison with the new nets. Two mid-depth smelt nets were added to each basin in 1998 to ensure that the entire water column from the thermocline (at about 30 ft) to very deep water was sampled.

These smelt gillnet investigations showed that smelt catches averaged 130/standard smelt net from 1987 through 1995. Smelt numbers declined from 1996 through 2005, averaging 35/standard smelt net, but then rebounded to 128/smelt net in 2006 and 140/standard smelt net in 2007. Smelt numbers were lower in 2008 and 2009 at 63.3 and 78.4 per smelt net, respectively.

In most investigations on Burntside Lake, smelt numbers were highest in the East End and lowest in the North Arm. However, in 2006, 2007, and 2008, smelt numbers were evenly distributed in each of the three basins of Burntside Lake. Smelt numbers in 2009 again were highest in the East End and lowest in the North Arm. As in most recent investigations on this lake, most of the smelt captured in 2009 (96 percent) were caught in the 3/8" bar mesh. Smelt sizes in 2009 averaged 4.9 inches; the largest was 8.8 inches.

Also captured in the smelt gillnets in 2009 were 7 slimy sculpin and one lake trout. The lake trout (8.4", right ventral clip) had been stocked as a yearling in 2008.

OTHER COLD WATER FISH POPULATIONS

Lake trout have been stocked into Burntside Lake since 1916. Since 1988 about 70,000 Gillis Lake strain lake trout yearlings have been stocked in Burntside Lake every other year. Since 1984 all stocked lake trout have been fin-clipped for later identification, to determine their survival and growth, and to monitor for the presence of unclipped trout that were produced by natural reproduction.

The lake trout catch rate in 2009 (1.7/gillnet) was slightly lower than the median catch of 2.2/gillnet in all deep water investigations on this lake. Lake trout sizes in 2009 averaged 15.0 inches (1.71 lbs), which was similar to the average size of 14.6 inches for all investigations on this lake. The largest lake trout captured in 2009 was 30.5 inches, which was also the largest caught in a gillnet in all Burntside Lake assessments. Twelve of 17 lake trout stomachs examined in 2009 were empty, 3 contained smelt, and 2 contained slimy sculpins. Six of the lake trout had anchor worms attached to them.

Of the 21 lake trout captured in the standard deep gillnets and the smelt nets in 2009, 18 were fin clipped, indicating they had been stocked. Two of the unclipped lake trout were aged by sectioning their otoliths, and the third was aged using an age-length key. Of the three unclipped lake trout, two (18.1" and 18.5") were age 7+ from the 2002 year class and the third (22.4") was age 8+ from the 2001 year class.

The presence of unclipped trout indicates that natural recruitment of lake trout is occurring. The proportion of naturally produced lake trout in the deep gillnet and smelt gillnet catches has increased in recent investigations, from 11 percent (3 of 27) in 2001, to 23 percent (6 of 26) in 2003, 33 percent (9 of 27) in 2005, and 54 percent (14 of 26) in 2007. Fourteen percent (3 of 21) of the lake trout caught in 2009 were unclipped.

Considering both stocked and naturally produced lake trout in Burntside Lake, age 1+ and 2+ lake trout growth rates were typical for lake trout lakes in the Tower Fisheries Management Area, while age 3+ and older growth rates were faster than normal. The faster growth of older trout may be due to the abundant smelt population available as forage.

The lake whitefish population in 2009 continued a trend of nonexistent recruitment, resulting in declining numbers and increasing sizes. Burntside Lake is located northwest of Ely and has five public motor boat accesses as well as a number of portage and water route connections to other nearby lakes. It is a 7,314 acre lake with a maximum depth of 126 feet and clear water. There are several relatively minor inlets, located mostly on the north side of the lake. The Shagawa River is the only outlet which flows out of the southwest corner of the lake where it then turns and heads east to Shagawa Lake. Burntside Lake is a two-story fishery with deep, cold, well oxygenated water capable of supporting a cold water fishery (fish such as lake trout, lake whitefish, cisco and burbot) and a shallow, warmer, but still well oxygenated area capable of supporting a cool and warm water fishery (fish such as walleye, northern pike, bass and panfish). Unfortunately, rainbow smelt and spiny water flea, both non-native invasive species are also present in Burntside Lake. Rainbow smelt were first discovered in the lake in 1970. Their presence is likely a result of an unintended bait release or the consequence of smelt netters cleaning their catch from Lake Superior on their docks and unintentionally introducing fertilized eggs to the lake. Spiny water flea are a zooplankton that were first discovered in Burntside Lake in 2010. Their presence is likely a result of infested boats or fishing equipment being used on Burntside. There is an increased risk of spread with this small invasive as they can attach to fishing lines, downriggers, anchor ropes and fishing nets, as well as be transported in bait buckets, bilges and livewells of boats if they are not completely dried out. Burntside is one of the most popular lakes in the Tower area providing for a number of recreational pursuits. It is a prototypical northern Minnesota/Canadian shield waterbody with shorelines covered in tall pines, areas of tall granite ledge rock, many islands, exceptionally clear water and much of the shoreline undeveloped. Areas along the south shore, east end and parts of the north arm are accessible by road. Some of these areas are moderately developed with homes and cabins. Most of the undeveloped public land is owned by the US Forest Service. Several lakeshore campsites are located on the north arm and west end. In the spring of 2015 the Forest Service conducted prescribed burns along the north shore of much of the west end and part of the southwest side of the north arm. Some of the islands on the west end were also burned. Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline are mostly boulder and ledgerock. Some bays have soft bottoms with a fair amount of aquatic vegetation. Additionally, a few bays are quite sandy and make for great swimming areas. Burntside has a long history of stocking dating back to 1912. Since 1965, walleye and lake trout were the only species that were stocked. Lake trout were stocked from the 1990's to 2010. Walleye fingerlings are still currently being stocked in even years at around 25,000 fish per stocking. This survey used four different net types: deep water gill nets, shallow water gill nets, small mesh gill nets and trap nets. Fish species sampled included black crappie, bluegill, burbot, golden shiner, green sunfish, hybrid sunfish, lake trout, lake whitefish, northern pike, rainbow smelt, rock bass, sculpin, shorthead redhorse, smallmouth bass, walleye, white sucker and yellow perch. The deep water gillnet catch for lake trout was just over one fish per net, down slightly from other assessments on Burntside Lake, and just below average when compared to other area trout lakes. Fish from 9 to 27 inches were sampled with an average length of 15 inches. The largest fish sampled and the average length are on par with previous surveys. The average weight was nearly two pounds. In 2010, lake trout stocking was discontinued, but all lake trout stocked prior to this had been fin-clipped for later age identification. Of the 22 lake trout captured in the 2015 assessment, only one fish was fin clipped. This indicated over 95% of the fish captured were naturally reproduced. Lake trout ranged in age from 2 to 12 years. Fish over 17 inches long or older than 6 years generally were sexually mature. Growth for young fish on Burntside was slightly slower but older fish was slightly faster compared to other trout populations in the Tower area. Lake whitefish in Burntside first started showing declines starting in 1982 and the 2015 catch rate was the lowest on record. Only six lake whitefish were caught in all the nets combined. Sizes ranged from 23 to 27 inches with an average of 25 inches. Ages of all six fish ranged from 24 to 54 years old, indicating that there has been little to no natural reproduction for the last 25 years. The average weight was just over 6 pounds and the largest whitefish weighed in at nearly 9.5 pounds. Cisco (tullibee) are noticeable by their absence from surveys since 1999. An average of 4 fish/deep gill net were captured from 1950 through 1986. Cisco numbers then gradually declined until 1997 when the last cisco was sampled. Declines of cisco and lake whitefish were likely due to the smelt introduction. The deep water gillnet catch for burbot was nearly a half a fish per net which was slightly better than average for Burntside Lake. Sizes were 20 to 24 inches with and average length of 22 inches. Although lake whitefish are on the decline and cisco seem to have disappeared completely, the burbot catch has remained relatively unchanged through time. Sixty-five walleye were sampled in the shallow water gill nets for a catch rate of just over five fish per net which is better than the historic average for Burntside Lake. Lengths ranged from 7 to 29 inches with an average of 16 inches which was slightly better than the average. The average weight was two pounds. Walleye growth in Burntside Lake is exceptional, likely due to the presence of smelt as a forage. Fish from 1 to 20 years old were sampled with all but the two oldest fish coming from a stocked year class. Ten year classes were identified with 2012, a stocked year, representing just over 50% of the catch. The northern pike shallow water gillnet catch was just over two fish per net which is better than average for Burntside Lake. Lengths ranged from 12 to 38 inches with an average of 25 inches. Both the average and maximum lengths were on par with previous surveys. The average weight was over four pounds. Twelve smallmouth bass were sampled in shallow water gill nets. Lengths ranged from 6 to 19 inches with an average of 11 inches. Thirty-three smallmouth were also sampled in trap nets for a catch rate of just over two fish per net which is the highest on record for the lake and quite high when compared to other similar lakes. The trapnetted fish tended to be a little smaller than fish from the gill nets. Growth was slow compared to other smallmouth bass populations in the area. Ages ranged from 3 to 10 years. The bluegill trapnet catch in 2015 was over 11 fish/net which is much higher than the two previous surveys that used trap nets. Sizes were relatively small though ranging from 3 to 8 inches with an average of 5 inches. The yellow perch shallow gillnet catch was just under one fish per net which is average for the lake. The lengths ranged from 8 to 10 inches. These sizes are comparable to previous surveys. High catches of rock bass were sampled in both shallow gill nets and trap nets. The shallow gill net catch rate was the highest catch rate on record for the lake. Combining the catches of both nets, lengths ranged from 4 to 9 inches with an average of 6 inches. Other species sampled in nets but in low numbers were black crappie, green sunfish, hybrid sunfish (pumpkinseed and northern sunfish cross), shorthead redhorse, sculpin, golden shiner and white sucker. Rainbow smelt are a non-native invasive fish that were first documented in Burntside Lake in 1970. Regular small-mesh gillnetting began in 1987. Previous surveys of smelt catches were highly variable but more recent assessments are showing lower numbers. The 2015 assessment shows the lowest catch rate to date. Sizes have remained relatively constant through time though. It is likely that the unintentional introduction of smelt has resulted in the nearly total failure of natural reproduction of walleye, lake whitefish, and cisco in Burntside Lake. Lake trout natural reproduction was also poor and has only recently showed signs of rebounding. These are all species that do not nest or otherwise protect their eggs or young following spawning. Smelt have been shown to have effects on these other species both by preying on eggs or young fish and by competing with these species for food. Spiny water flea (Bythotrephes longimanus) are a non-native invasive zooplankton that were first discovered in Burntside Lake in 2010. They are known to consume other native zooplankton which are often an important food source for native fish. Evidence from other lakes has shown a decline or elimination of some species of native zooplankton after spiny's were introduced. There is an increased risk of spread with this small invasive as they can attach to fishing lines, downriggers, anchor ropes, and fishing nets, as well as be transported in bait buckets, bilges and livewells of boats if they are not completely dried out. Although they were only recently introduced to Burntside Lake, their impacts have yet to be determined. During the 2015 winter trout season a creel survey was conducted on Burntside Lake. The purpose was to obtain estimates of current angling pressure, catch, harvest and release rates, as well as gather information on the population of stocked versus naturally reproduced lake trout. Results from the creel were summarized into the Burntside Lake 2015 Winter Creel Survey Completion Report. Survey results were not available at the time of this report.

Walleye fingerlings are currently being stocked on an every even year basis at an average rate of nearly 25,000 fish per stocking event. This was likely a result of an unintended bait release or the consequence of smelt netters cleaning their catch from Lake Superior on their docks and unintentionally introducing fertilized eggs to the lake.

The overall deep water gillnet catch rate for all fish combined was 2.2 fish/net which was below average compared to past surveys on the lake. Yield was 6.0 lbs/net which was also below the lakes historic average. Fish species sampled in deep water gill nets were lake trout, lake whitefish, burbot, and rainbow smelt. The overall shallow water gillnet catch rate for all fish combined was 13.3 fish/net which was below the lakes historic average. Yield however was 24.7 lbs/net which was above average. The overall small-mesh gillnet catch rate for all fish combined was 2.6 fish/net which was the lowest catch rate on record for the lake, although this maintains a similar trend of the past several surveys showing a decreasing catch rate driven mostly by rainbow smelt numbers. The deep water gillnet catch rate for lake trout in 2021 was 1.0 fish/net which was below average compared to historic surveys of Burntside. This catch rate was also below average compared to all other lake trout lakes in the Tower area. Lengths ranged from 7 to 28 inches with an average of nearly 20 inches. This average length was the best since the 1988 survey. Maximum length was on par with previous surveys and the average fish weighed nearly 3 pounds. Aging was not done on all lake trout that were caught, but of those that were, ages ranged from 1 to 8 years. Growth was fast when compared to the averages of all lake trout lakes in the Tower area. The average seven year old lake trout was 20 inches long.

Ten lake whitefish were caught in the deep water gillnets for a catch rate of 0.8 fish/net. The lake whitefish population appears to be slowly rebounding after hitting a low catch rate of 0.3 fish/deep net in 2015. The prior declining population was likely due to the introduction and expansion of rainbow smelt, first documented in the 1970's. Sizes of all lake whitefish sampled in 2021 were 5.5 to nearly 28 inches with an average of 15 inches. Ages ranged from 2 to 27 with 13 of the 15 fish under the age of nine. This was by far the most young, small, fish that were sampled since the late 1980's.

Forty-six walleye were sampled in the shallow water gill nets for a catch rate of 3.8 fish/net. This catch rate was slightly below average for Burntside Lake. Lengths ranged from 7 to 27 inches with an average of just over 18 inches. This average length was the second longest on record for the lake. The average weight was 2.5 pounds. Walleye growth was good compared to other lakes in the area with the average fish taking only four years to reach 16 inches long. Ages ranged from 1 to 23 with nearly all fish coming from stocked years. Eight year classes were identified with the 2016 year class containing nearly half of the total catch.

The northern pike shallow water gillnet catch was 2.7 fish/net which was tied with two other surveys for the highest catch rate on record for the lake. Lengths ranged from 15 to 41 inches with an average of nearly 24 inches. Sizes were on par with previous surveys and the average weight was 3.5 pounds.

Seventeen smallmouth bass were sampled in shallow water gill nets for a catch rate of 1.4 fish/net which was average for the lake. Lengths ranged from 6 to 19 inches with an average of just over 12 inches. Growth however was quite slow with the average fish taking seven years to reach 12 inches long. Ages ranged from 2 to 16 years.

The small mesh gillnet catch rate of rainbow smelt was 1.8 fish/net. This was the lowest catch rate on record for the lake. Previous surveys of smelt catches were highly variable, however the catch rate has shown a dramatic drop over the past five surveys. Sizes have remained relatively constant through time with an overall average length of 5 inches. This however isn't surprising as the mesh size is highly selective for specific sizes of fish. If the overall size distribution has become smaller, as appears is the case based on stomach analysis of predator fish, the small mesh nets would likely still sample the same sizes of individual fish that have been sampled in the past. However, if the true mean size has shrunk, the majority of the fish may simply be small enough to swim through the smallest mesh size and thus aren't sampled.

Smallmouth sizes in 2003 averaged 13.5", which was larger than the average size of 11.6" in all investigations on this lake. Smallmouth scales were used for age and growth analysis and were considered to be easy to read. It appeared that seven year classes of smallmouth were captured in 2003, but that recruitment was erratic. Smallmouth growth was somewhat faster than normal (in the third quartile) by area standards.Rock bass numbers in 2003 (7.4/gillnet) were similar to the median catch of 6.3/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Other fish species were present in low numbers in the shallow water gillnets in 2003.Neascus was found on about half of the northern pike, yellow perch, and smallmouth bass and a third of the walleye examined in 2003. Bass tapeworm larvae were found in the viscera of about half of the smallmouth bass. Yellow grubs were found in about half of the yellow perch.Deep Water Fish Populations:Deep water fish populations in 2003, similar to recent investigations, were dominated by rainbow smelt and lake trout. The total catch of smelt in the smelt gillnets has declined from their peak numbers in the late 1980's but are still quite abundant. The total catch of fish (all species combined) in the deep gillnets in 2003 of 3.1 fish/net (9.6 lb/net) was lower than the median catch of 7.4 fish/net (11.2 lb/net) in all deep water investigations on this lake, due to lower numbers of lake whitefish and the absence of cisco.Rainbow smelt were first observed in Burntside Lake in 1972, and regular smelt assessment gillnetting began in 1987 with nets that had 1/2" or 3/8" bar multifilament mesh that were 6' high, but were odd lengths (150' or 195' long). Smelt gillnets were standardized in 1992 at 200', with each net consisting of one 6' x 100' x 3/8" bar nylon multifilament mesh panel and one 6' x 100' x 1/2" bar nylon multifilament mesh panel. Net set depths and locations were standardized in 1990, with six deep nets (two nets each on the East Arm, North Arm, and West Arm). Two additional nets were added at mid-depth locations in each basin in 1998 to ensure the entire water column from the thermocline (at about 30' and 55 F) to the bottom was sampled. Net catches prior to 1992 were converted to standard smelt net 200' equivalents to facilitate comparison with later standard net catches.After their introduction, smelt catches increased to high numbers, averaging 130/standard smelt net from 1987 through 1995. Smelt numbers declined after 1995 and have averaged 35/net from 1996 through 2003. Smelt numbers have increased again in the last few years, however, and 75/net were captured in 2003. Smelt numbers increased in each basin of the lake in 2003, but especially in the west end where 134/net were captured. Similar to recent investigations, 99 percent of the smelt in 2003 were captured in the 3/8" bar mesh. Smelt sizes in 2003 averaged 4.7"; the largest was 6.8".Also captured in the smelt nets in 2003 were six lake trout and six sculpins. The lake trout ranged in size from 8.0" to 24.0". All six lake trout had fin clips indicating they had been stocked. Lake trout have been stocked for many decades in Burntside Lake. Lake trout numbers in the deep gillnets in 2003 (1.7/net) were similar to the median catch of 2.2/gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Lake trout sizes in the deep gillnets in 2003 averaged 15.5" (2.1 lb), which was larger than the average size of 14.5" in all investigations on this lake. The largest lake trout captured in 2003 was 30.3". Fourteen lake trout stomachs examined in 2003 were empty, two contained smelt, one contained sculpins, and one contained a smallmouth bass. Anchor worms (small parasites which attach to the skin or gills) were found on a few of the lake trout examined in 2003.Of the 26 lake trout captured in both deep gillnets and smelt nets in 2003, 20 had clipped fins indicating they had been stocked. One of the unclipped trout had crystallized otoliths, indicating it also had been stocked, but had been missed during clipping operations or had received an incomplete clip that subsequently regenerated (crystallized otoliths are common in hatchery reared yearling lake trout). Five trout, ranging in size from 21" to 30" were unclipped, indicating they were naturally produced or had been missed during clipping operations. Since all lake trout stocked in Burntside Lake after 1984 have been fin-clipped, it is unlikely that any of the unclipped trout (except, perhaps, the 30" trout) would have come from stockings in 1984 or earlier. In general, the lake trout captured in Burntside Lake in 2003 were growing faster than the median for 12 lake trout lakes in the Tower Fisheries Management Area.Fourteen of the 26 lake trout captured in deep water gillnets and smelt nets in 2003 were age four, and had been stocked as yearlings in the spring of 2000. Thirteen of these trout were fin-clipped (the other one had crystallized otoliths). Most of these trout (8 of 13) had adipose & left pelvic fin clips and were wild progeny of eggs and sperm taken at Gillis Lake the fall of 1998. These fish averaged 13.1" at recapture and were from a relatively small stocking of 16,000 yearlings that were fairly large (averaging 9.3/lb) when stocked in the spring of 2000.The remainder of these lake trout (5 of 13) had left pelvic fin clips and were the progeny of Gillis Lake strain brood stock raised in the hatchery system. These fish were smaller, averaging 12.6" at recapture, and were from a much larger stocking of 54,539 yearlings that were smaller (averaging 11.7/lb) when stocked in the spring of 2000. This limited data suggests a survival and growth advantage to the wild Gillis Lake yearlings that were larger at the time of stocking than the hatchery brood stock yearlings.The lake whitefish population in 2003 continued a trend of nonexistent recruitment, resulting in declining numbers and increasing sizes. Whitefish numbers averaged 9.5/deep gillnet from 1950 through 1981, declined to an average of 5.2/deep gillnet through 1985, then gradually declined to the 2003 abundance of 0.9/deep gillnet. Whitefish sizes gradually increased during this time, from an average of 14.1" in 1950 and 1968, to an average of 23.8" in 2003. No whitefish under 21" were caught in 2003.Cisco have apparently been extirpated from this lake. An average of 4.1 cisco/deep gillnet were captured from 1950 through 1986. Cisco numbers then gradually declined, and no cisco have been captured in the last three deep gillnet assessments. We feel that the introduction of smelt has resulted in the nearly total failure of natural recruitment of walleye, lake trout, lake whitefish, and cisco in Burntside Lake. These are all cold water spawning species that do not nest or otherwise protect their eggs after spawning. The literature has many examples of similar recruitment failures in lakes stocked with smelt (e.g. Evans and Loftus, 1987. Colonization of inland lakes in the Great Lakes region by rainbow smelt. International Symposium of Stocks Assessment and Yield Prediction, Vol 44, Supplement 2. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences. Vol 44, Supplement 2:249-266). The mechanisms by which smelt affect recruitment of other species may be direct (by eating eggs or young fish) or indirect (by competing for forage, particularly invertebrate forage).

Temperature and dissolved oxygen (DO) measurements were collected from the deepest basin in Burntside Lake on August 20th, 2025, to evaluate the quantity and quality of cold, oxygenated water (i.e., oxythermal habitat) available to Lake Trout, the most sensitive coldwater species present in this lake (lake Whitefish and Cisco, also known as Tulibee are present). During the summer, Lake Trout require a layer of oxythermal habitat that contains water temperatures below 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) and dissolved oxygen concentrations above 3.0 mg/L. Based on the profile from the deepest basin (maximum sampled depth 124.6 feet), the water temperature decreased below 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) at 43.3 feet and the dissolved oxygen concentration decreased to 3.0 mg/L at 113.0 feet at the time of sampling. The thickness of this layer of water in the water column was 69.7 feet, indicating that oxythermal habitat was present for Lake Trout.

Further, the temperature at which dissolved oxygen decreased to 3.0 mg/L (i.e., TDO3, a single variable to characterize oxythermal habitat) was 4.7 degrees C (40.5 degrees F). TDO3 values cooler than 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) indicate that oxythermal conditions were suitable for Lake Trout at the time of the survey.

Data collected by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources during the late summer period of maximum oxythermal stress (July 26th to Aug 24th) in 2011 and 2024 also indicate suitable oxythermal habitat. When inadequate oxythermal habitat is available, Lake Trout are squeezed into unfavorable, warmer water conditions and experience higher levels of stress.

Burntside Lake is located approximately 6 miles NW of Ely, MN. It has a surface area of 7,139 acres and a maximum depth of 126 feet. There are several public accesses located around the lake. Burntside is designated as infested waters because of the presence of spiny water flea.
Burntside has a long history of lake trout stocking and recent findings indicate that natural reproduction is improving. For this special assessment we targeted 4 of the known spawning reefs with the purpose of collecting DNA for genetic testing.
A total of 57 mature lake trout (1.02/net) were sampled using 3/4" double pot trap nets. A total of 8 lake trout were fin clipped (7% male and 7% female) indicating Gillis Lake ancestry and the remaining 49 trout had no visible fin clips. Mean length was 26.0" and the largest lake trout sampled was 32.0".
From 1990 through 1998 seven special assessments were conducted on these same 4 spawning reefs and others on Burntside Lake. Catch rates were similar and the catch of fin clipped lake trout ranged from 5.0% to 51.6%.

Burntside Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large and deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (unmineralized) water. Burntside Lake is typical of these lakes, except that it is smaller (7,139 acres) than the lake class average of 29,503 acres. Burntside Lake was thermally stratified on 07/19/99 and retained good oxygen levels for fish (more than 5 ppm) to within a few feet of the bottom, where the temperature was 40 F. The water clarity and oxygen and temperature profiles in 1999 were similar to previous investigations on this lake. Fish populations in 1999 were investigated with shallow gillnets, deep gillnets, and smelt gillnets. The shallow gillnets were set in depths of 8-28 ft, where the water temperatures were warmer than 55 F. The deep gillnets were set in depths of 60-95 ft, where the water temperatures were colder than 55 F. The smelt nets were special small mesh gillnets (50 ft each of 1/2" bar mesh and 3/8" bar mesh), and were set in depths of 35-92 ft, where the water temperatures were also colder than 55 F. Stratified shallow and deep gillnet sets differ from "standard" gillnet sets, which may be set from shallow-to-deep water and can capture both warm water and cold water fish species. Because lake class quartiles were developed for "standard" gillnet sets, their use is not appropriate for comparison with stratified gillnet sets and they are not presented in the report. Shallow Water Fish Populations Shallow water fish populations in 1999 were dominated by walleye, northern pike, rock bass, and smallmouth bass. Walleye numbers in 1999 (6.3/net) were higher than the median catch of 3.7/net in fourteen previous shallow water investigations on this lake dating back to 1950. Walleye numbers have been higher than normal for this lake since 1990, due to biennial stockings of about 12 large walleye fingerlings per littoral acre. Walleye sizes in 1999 averaged 17.3" (2.4 lb); the largest walleye was 26.8" (7.4 lb). Sixty-nine of 76 walleye captured in 1999 were from fingerling-stocked year classes. Natural reproduction of walleye in Burntside Lake has been poor for many years and may be related to the introduction of smelt around 1970. Of 75 walleye stomachs examined in 1999, 57 were empty and 18 contained smelt. Growth of walleye captured in 1999 was in the fourth quartile for area lakes. Northern pike numbers in 1999 (2.7/net) were higher than the median catch of 1.6/net in previous investigations on this lake. Pike sizes in 1999 averaged 23.0" (3.9 lb); the largest was 44.9" (22 lb). Of 33 northern pike stomachs examined, 23 were empty, 7 contained smelt, 1 contained smallmouth bass, 1 contained rock bass, and 1 contained unidentified fish remains. Pike growth was in the fourth quartile for area lakes. Rock bass numbers in 1999 (8.3/net) were higher than the median catch of 5.6/net in previous investigations on this lake . Rock bass numbers appeared to increase about 1980 and have been fairly high since then. Rock bass sizes in 1999 averaged 6.4"; the largest was 8.7". Smallmouth bass numbers in 1999 (1.8/net) were higher than the median catch of 1.0/net in previous investigations on this lake. DNR records indicate "bass" were stocked in 1941, however no smallmouth were observed in the initial 1950 lake survey. Smallmouth were captured in the following investigation, in 1968. A 1999 summer creel survey indicated an abundant smallmouth population, with many small bass caught by anglers. Smallmouth sizes in the gillnets in 1999 averaged 11.5" (1.0 lb); the largest was 20.3". Deep Water Fish Populations Deep water fish populations in 1999 were dominated by lake trout, lake whitefish, and rainbow smelt. Lake trout numbers in 1999 (3.2/net) were higher than the median catch of 2.2/net in 18 previous deep water investigations on this lake dating back to 1950. Lake trout numbers since 1990 have been enhanced by the biennial stocking of about 10 lake trout yearlings per surface acre. Lake trout sizes in 1999 averaged 14.1"; the largest was 28.2". Thirty of the 37 lake trout captured in 1999 were fin-clipped, stocked fish. Four trout, ranging from age four (11.7") to age 15 (27.8") had no discernable fin-clips. Two trout had confusing clips that could not be associated with known clips. Of the fin-clipped trout, six were from the 1997 year class and had grown from an average size of 6.6" when stocked in May of 1998 to an average size of 8.8" when recaptured 14 months later. Twenty three were from the 1995 year class and had grown from an average size of 7.1" when stocked in May of 1996 to an average size of 12.8" when recaptured 38 months later. One was from the 1993 year class and had grown from an average size of of 7.2" when stocked in May of 1994 to 22.0" when recaptured 62 months later. The growth of the stocked trout from the 1997 and 1995 year classes was normal by area standards. Of 38 lake trout stomachs examined, 20 contained smelt, 10 were empty, 4 contained sculpins, and 4 contained unidentified fish remains. The lake whitefish population in 1999 continued a trend of declining numbers and increasing sizes, both due to a lack of recruitment. Whitefish numbers averaged 9.5/net from 1950 through 1981, declined to an averaged of 5.2/net through 1985, and then gradually declined to the 1999 abundance of 1.2/net. Whitefish average lengths gradually increased during this time, from an average of 14.1" in 1950 and 1968, to an average of 22.8" in 1999. No whitefish under 20" were captured in 1999. The cisco population followed the same trend as the whitefish population. Cisco numbers averaged 4.1/net from 1950 through 1986, then gradually declined to the 1997 abundace of 0.1/net. No cisco were captured in 1999. Rainbow smelt were first observed in Burntside Lake in 1972, and increased to quite high numbers, averaging 130 per smelt net from 1987 through 1995. Smelt numbers declined following 1995 and have averaged 20/net in the last four investigations. The 1999 catch was 20.6/net. Higher numbers of smelt were caught in the west end of the lake (30.7/net) and the east arm (27.2/net) than in the north arm (6.5/net). Eighty-six percent of the smelt were caught in the 3/8" mesh, a figure comparable to most previous catches on this lake. Smelt sizes in 1999, also comparable to most previous catches, averaged 4.8"; the largest was 8.4".

Burntside Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large and deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (unmineralized) water. Burntside Lake is smaller and has clearer water than typical for this lake class.

Burntside Lake was thermally stratified on 07/14/2008 with surface temperatures of 63 F and bottom temperatures of 44 F. This surface temperature was about 5 F cooler than typical for mid-July. Adequate oxygen for trout (more than 5 ppm) was retained to within five feet of the bottom in each of the three major basins (North Arm, East End, West End) of this lake. The water quality in 2008 was similar to previous investigations on this lake that showed Burntside Lake was an oligotrophic lake with excellent water quality and low water fertility.

Smelt were first observed in Burntside Lake in 1970 and a variety of gillnets were used to catch smelt through the mid 1980's. Regular smelt assessment gillnetting began in 1987 at standard locations (two nets in each of the three major basins on the lake) with nets that were 6 feet x 100 feet x 0.5 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon and 6 feet x 150 feet (or 200 feet) x 0.375 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon. Standard smelt nets (200 feet x 6 feet with one 100 foot panel of 0.375 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon and one 100 foot panel of 0.5 inch bar mesh multifilament nylon) were introduced in 1992 and previous 0.375 inch bar mesh catches were converted to 100 foot equivalents for purposes of comparison with the new nets. Two mid depth smelt nets were added to each major basin in 1998 to ensure that the entire water column from the thermocline (at about 25 feet) to deep water was sampled.

These smelt investigations showed that smelt catches averaged 130/standard smelt net through the mid 1990's. Smelt numbers then declined, averaging 35/standard smelt net from 1996 through 2005 (the 2005 smelt catch was 12/standard smelt net). This decline appeared to show that our strategy of stocking walleye fingerlings and lake trout yearlings was reducing the smelt population through predation. However smelt numbers then rebounded, to 128/net in 2006, 140/net in 2007, and 63/net in 2008.

The distribution of smelt within the major basins of the lake was similar to recent investigations, with the highest catch of smelt (84/net) in the East End, followed by 54/net in the North Arm and 52/net in the West End.

Also similar to most recent assessments, 98 percent (743 of 758) of the smelt captured in 2008 were in the 0.375 inch bar mesh. Smelt sizes in 2008 averaged 5.0 inches; the largest smelt was 7.3 inches.

Also captured in the smelt nets in 2006 were four lake trout and nineteen slimy sculpin. Two of the lake trout (18.5" and 20.2") had clipped right ventral fins, indicating they had been stocked in 2004 as yearlings. The unclipped trout were 5.2" and 22.0".

Burntside Lake is located approximately 6 miles northwest of Ely within the Superior National Forest. This scenic lake is well known for its clear water and rocky, pine covered shorelines with numerous islands. Most of the development has occurred along the south and east shores. Another area of development can be found along the north shore. Several resorts and camps are also present. Burntside Lake is considered as infested waters with the discovery of spiny water fleas in 2010.

There are several options for public access including various boat ramps and also portages from nearby lakes and rivers. There are 5 US Forest Service administered campsites on the lake for overnight or day use.

A targeted lake survey on Burntside Lake was completed during the week of 7/16-25/18. The primary focus was on the deepwater fish community. Twelve standard experimental gill nets were used and another 12 small mesh gill nets were set targeting smelt. Lake trout, lake whitefish and one burbot were sampled in the standard gill nets. Rainbow smelt, sculpin and one 6 inch lake trout were sampled in the smelt nets.

Lake trout numbers in 2018 (1.1/gill net) were similar to the historic average (1.7/gill net) for Burntside Lake. Lake trout average length was 16.2 inches which is slightly larger than the historic average length of 15.2 inches. Lake trout sizes ranged from 6 inches to a maximum of 28.4 inches. Ten lake trout were aged with representation from 6 different years from ages 3 to 16. Lake trout were last stocked in 2010.

Lake whitefish numbers in 2018 (0.7/gill net) were lower than the historic average (2.6/gill net). Whitefish average length was 22.3 inches which is larger than the historic average length of 19.8 inches. Whitefish sizes ranged from 15.9 inches up to a maximum of 30.2 inches, which is the largest whitefish sampled from Burntside Lake to date. Eight whitefish were aged with representation from 7 different years from ages 4 to 48.

Rainbow smelt abundance in 2018 (2.5/gill net) was much lower than the historic average (62.7/gill net) and in fact was the lowest catch of smelt since the sampling was standardized. Smelt average length was 5.2 inches which is similar to the historic average length of 5.0 inches. Smelt sizes ranged from 3.8 inches to a maximum of 8.5 inches. Rainbow smelt are a non-native fish species that were first sampled in 1970.

This resurvey included shallow gillnetting, trapnetting, and shoreline seining. Deep water gillnetting and deep water smelt netting were also conducted in 1995 but were reported as separate assessments. One of the dryest summers on record was experienced in 1995, with many local wildfires reported. The water level on Burntside lake was low, and many of the inlets which normally have flowing water were dry.Many types of aquatic plants were identified during the survey; but all were rated as being rare, indicating the lake has very little vegetation overall. Boulders and rubble dominated shallow water substrates. Shoreline seining in sandy areas captured only two young smallmouth bass - a much poorer catch than in most lakes.Most shallow gillnetting was done at depths shallower than 21', at which point water temperatures were about 55 F. The total number of fish caught (all species combined) in the gillnets was typical for lakes of this type, except that the presence of many large walleye increased the total weight of fish caught to above average. The total number of fish caught in the trapnets was average, but the presence of many small rock bass decreased the total weight of fish caught to below average.Walleye were the dominant species in the gillnet catch. All walleye were from stocked year-classes, indicating that natural reproduction has been unsuccessful despite the high number of spawning age walleye that are present. Walleye fingerlings have been stocked on an every-other-year basis for some time. Walleye numbers and weight were above average for this type of lake.All walleye were in excellent condition and had lots of fat stored in their body cavities. Twenty nine percent of walleye stomachs contained smelt, the rest were empty. Walleye growth was extremely fast: 14.5" at age three and 20" at age five.Rock bass and smallmouth bass were abundant in both the gillnets and the trapnets. Smallmouth growth appeared to be slow, and few were present from 1993 or 1992. Average numbers of northern pike, white sucker, and shorthead redhorse were present. Northern pike appeared to be growing well and reproducing regularily. Below average numbers of bluegill were present, and most were small. No bluegill from 1992 through 1995 were present. Bluegill growth was average. Also present were low numbers of green sunfish, golden shiner, and yellow perch. SMELT NETS:Six small mesh (100' of 0.5" bar mesh and 100' of 0.375" bar mesh) gillnets were set in 1995 to assess smelt populations. Two nets were set in each of the three major basins at sites standardized since 1987. Nets were set in water depths of 60' to 90'. Water temperatures at these depths ranged from 41 F to 37 F and oxygen levels ranged from 9.0 ppm to 5.4 ppm.The six nets caught an average of 116 smelt per net. All but three of the smelt were caught in the smaller 0.375" mesh. The average size of the smelt was 4.8", but four larger smelt, up to 8.9" were also caught. Notable by their absence in this assessment were sculpins, low numbers of which have been caught in previous smelt assessments.More smelt were caught in the East Arm (180 per net) than in the West End (108 per net) or in the North Arm (60 per net). Smelt were found at all depths sampled (60' - 90'). DEEP NETS:Deep water fish populations in 1995 were evaluated with 12 standard deep water gillnet sets and six deep water smelt gillnets (reported separately). A resurvey, including shallow gillnets, trapnets, and shoreline seining, was also conducted in 1995 and is reported separately.The standard deep gillnets were set in the three major basins of the lake (East Arm, West End, and North Arm), at depths of 60' to 90', at water temperatures of 41 F to 35 F, and at oxygen levels of 9.0 ppm to 5.4 ppm.These gillnet sets show deep water fish populations dominated by lake trout and lake whitefish. The smelt population (reported separately), is also fairly numerous. One cisco and one burbot were also captured during the deep water gillnetting.Most of the lake trout (41 of 43) were fin-clipped, indicating that they were stocked fish. Most of these (38 of 41) were from the previous two stockings of Gillis Lake strain yearlings in 1994 and 1992. The 1994 stocked trout had grown from about 7.5" at the time of stocking to an average of 9.0" when recaptured during this assessment 14 months after stocking. The 1992 stocked trout had grown from about 7.5" at the time of stocking to an average of 13.9" when recaptured during this assessment 38 months after stocking. Both the 1992 and 1994 stocked trout showed an apparent slowdown of growth in the last year; the reason for this is not known.Most of the trout stomachs examined were empty (53%), others contained smelt (35%), insects (5%), zooplankton (5%), or sculpins (2%).Whitefish sizes ranged from 17" to 24". The absence of small whitefish indicates a lack of successful reproduction of this species.
